text.title: Chaffinch
text.menu_sub: Sing from the treetops, flit between trees, pick seeds and beetles off the ground.
text.menu_wild: Foxes catch you on the ground.
text.intro: Hold Fly to climb, Dive to drop. Seeds and beetles are on the ground. Roost in tree leaves at night.
text.hungry: You're hungry. Hop about on the ground under the trees and look for seeds and beetles.
text.no_food: Nothing to eat here. Look for seeds under the spruces and birches, or beetles on the ground.
text.chased: A fox is after you! Fly up into a tree!
text.stalk_hint: A chaffinch pecking at the ground. Creep up slowly: it flies off if it sees you.
text.sings: A chaffinch is singing: a quick, falling trill with a flourish at the end.
text.nest_hint: A chaffinch nest, low in the spruce! Tap Pounce to reach it.
text.caught_eggs: You found a chaffinch nest and ate the eggs! +{food} food
text.caught_nestlings: You found a chaffinch nest and ate the nestlings! +{food} food
text.nest_alarm: Pink! Pink! The chaffinch parents call in alarm.
text.about_looks: A sparrow-sized finch with two white bars on each wing. The male has a blue-grey head and a pinkish-orange face and breast; the female is olive-brown.
text.about_food: Seeds of spruce, pine, birch and meadow plants, picked mostly off the ground. In summer, caterpillars, beetles and spiders.
text.about_home: Lives in every kind of forest. The female builds a neat cup of moss and grass, covered in lichen and spider silk, in the fork of a spruce or birch.
text.about_winter: Most fly to western and southern Europe in September and October and come back in April. A few males stay in Finland and visit bird feeders.
text.about_young: Four to six eggs in May, blue-grey with purple spots. The parents feed the nestlings caterpillars, and they leave the nest after two weeks, in June.
text.about_fact: Its Latin name, coelebs, means "bachelor". In winter in Sweden, Linnaeus saw only males: the females had flown further south.

sources: Svensson, L. et al.: Collins Bird Guide, 2nd ed. (2009)

year.shelter: Roosts in dense spruces and other trees. The female builds the nest in early May: a neat cup of moss, grass and roots, covered in lichen and bound with spider silk, in a tree fork 1–10 m up, often in a spruce or birch.
year.young: 4–6 eggs from mid-May; the female sits on them for about 13 days. The nestlings are fed caterpillars and leave the nest after about 14 days, mostly in June. Some pairs raise a second brood.

food.spring: Seeds on the ground (spruce, pine and birch seeds, last year's meadow plants), then the first insects.
food.summer: Caterpillars, beetles, flies and spiders from leaves and the ground; the nestlings get almost only insects.
food.autumn: Seeds again, often in flocks on fields and under trees, before flying south.
food.winter: Away: winters in western and southern Europe. A few males stay at bird feeders in southern Finland.

year.notes: Males arrive first, in late March or April, and sing from the treetops to claim their patch; the song is one of the first sounds of spring in Finland. Each male sings his own few song types, learned in his first spring. The alarm call is a loud 'pink!'. Nests are robbed by jays, crows, squirrels, martens and woodpeckers far more often than by foxes; a fox only reaches the lowest nests. Fledglings sit on low branches and the ground for a few days, where foxes and cats catch them. One of the commonest birds in Finland's forests.
